title: Two replies to Maya’s rollback alert

beats.say: Maya is on call. Payment latency has crossed the rollback threshold. Read just the first three words of each reply. Which preview tells her what to do?

The compact reply opens with “Stop the rollout.” Unfold both replies. The checklist starts with the threshold warning. Step one gives the same instruction. Both replies tell Maya to stop the rollout and run the rollback. One puts the action first. The other gives her two steps she can tick off.

Which layout is easier to follow? Give a language model the replies, Maya’s task and a rubric for clarity. Now the model can act as an LLM judge. Suppose the judge picks the checklist because the numbered actions are easy to scan.

We can swap the replies to see if it still picks the checklist, then ask on-call engineers how they’d vote. By the end, you’ll be able to trace a vote, measure agreement and coverage, and decide what evidence Maya still needs before acting.
The policy calls for rollback. Here are two records tied to the same policy version. Compare each action field with the allowed value, run rollback. Both match. Code can settle that question exactly.
Now read the sentences beside those fields. One says to run the rollback. The other says, “Do not run the rollback.” If we search both replies for the word rollback, which ones pass?

Both pass. The search found the word twice, once in each reply. The words “do not” reverse the second recommendation. An exact field check can pass while the prose contradicts the policy. To evaluate that prose, compare its meaning with the source.
Use a validated judge to assist that review, and send unfamiliar or high-consequence exceptions to the policy owner. Access and action permissions stay with the host.

title: How many judgments will this comparison take?

beats.say: Suppose Maya gets one reply. We can grade it on its own. That’s pointwise evaluation. Here, zero means a required action is missing, one means both appear but their order is unclear, and two means both actions and their order are clear. These are ordinal levels.
The numbers put answers in order. To average them, you’d have to explain how much improvement each step represents. One call per answer gives N judgments for N answers.

Put two replies side by side for the same task and you have a pairwise comparison. The six dots represent six prompt revisions. Each dot can meet five others. That counts each connecting line twice, so divide by two. You get fifteen unordered pairs. In general, multiply N by N minus one, then divide by two.

Showing both orders requires thirty calls per task. A fixed baseline uses N minus one pairs. Comparing the five alternatives only with one fixed baseline needs five pairs, or ten calls with swaps. What happens if we send a longer reference?

Suppose the input grows from two hundred tokens per call to eight hundred. The ten calls now read eight thousand input tokens instead of two thousand. That’s a different workload for the same number of calls.

A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A. These preferences cycle. They cannot give us a single ranking that respects every vote. A forced choice can also produce a winner when neither reply is supported. Allow joint rejection or review.

Reference guidance supplies an answer key or source evidence alongside either format. Here “permission” is a valid paraphrase of “approval.” Check each claim and its conditions. A short reference may omit other valid solutions. Prometheus used custom rubrics and reference answers. G-Eval studied criterion-based forms for summarization and dialogue.

JudgeLM learned GPT-four judgments using swap augmentation and reference techniques. Agreement with that teacher measures how well JudgeLM learned its preferences. To check a factual claim in Maya’s reply, open the policy it cites.

title: Write criteria a reviewer can apply

beats.say: Our fictional policy, DEP twenty-seven, says to stop the rollout and run the rollback procedure after a threshold is crossed. Candidate compact states both facts in one sentence. Candidate stepwise gives the same facts as two numbered actions.

A rubric can score whether both required actions appear, whether their order is clear, and whether an operator can scan them quickly. Give each level an example so reviewers know what a zero, one, and two mean.
For this example, assume a reviewer checked both replies against the policy. Keep the policy, answer text, rubric version, and judge configuration tied to each evaluation case.

title: Can this receipt enter the comparison?

beats.say: The host knows the case, the two reply versions and the order it sent. The model gets to return a verdict and evidence. Here’s one receipt. The verdict is B. Its evidence is a list containing a nonblank observation. Those are the only two fields.
The other permitted verdicts are A, tie and review. This receipt passes the shape check. We still have to check what the observation says.

Now slip another verdict into that same receipt. Read the two entries in order. The first says A and the second says B. What will Python’s default JSON decoder keep? Can the host safely count that as a vote?

Python keeps B, the last value. By the time you inspect the dictionary, A has disappeared. Give the decoder an object pairs hook so it sees both names before building the dictionary. It rejects the duplicate.
The same check catches a Unicode escape that spells the same field name after decoding. Keep the raw receipt as a parse failure. A failed parse supplies no vote.

The article’s strict decoder also rejects nonstandard numbers such as NaN and infinity, malformed JSON such as a trailing comma, and non-text input. Across its two exercises it rejects four bad JSON receipts and six malformed structured replies.

For a decoded object, reject extra fields, unknown verdicts, wrong types and empty or blank evidence. Record provider refusals, truncation and transport errors separately. Send only validated receipts into aggregation. Constructing the result object yourself can skip these checks.

Go back to the clean receipt. It says B leads with the action. Read B’s first sentence. It leads with the threshold warning. The receipt parses, but the reason misquotes the reply. Check the observation against the actual text before trusting it.
The host must bind the case and configuration IDs to the exact evidence, rubric, judge and settings. An ID alone can’t authenticate a record or grant access.

title: Does the model’s verdict follow from the policy?

beats.say: The article records a local Qwen-three run on seven claims. The model has one point seven billion parameters. Sampling and thinking were off. Read the human key beside those claims. It has two supported, two contradicted and three review labels.

The model recognized that permission means approval here. It also recognized the linked plan requirement, caught one contradiction and sent the planted instruction to review. These are the results recorded in the article.

Look at the claim that commander approval is optional. The model marked it supported. Now read its reason. It says that approval is required. It also approved two requirements the policy never states, one for security review and one for on-call approval. All three are valid JSON.
The smaller model in the article, with zero point six billion parameters, called every claim supported. Before relying on either judge, measure its mistakes on held-out claims for your own policy.

title: Which reply did the judge pick?

beats.say: Here are the two replies Maya saw. Compact is in A and stepwise is in B. Our first receipt says B. File that choice under stepwise. For the second call, slide the two replies into each other’s slots. The task, the wording, the rubric and the judge settings all stay fixed.
This receipt says A. Read A against the new order. Do the two receipts pick the same reply?
Yes. Both pick stepwise. B on the first call and A on the second call follow the numbered instructions. Record one preference for the pair. Whether a reviewer agrees is a separate question.
Replay just the second receipt. Keep the replies in their reversed positions. This time it says B. The first receipt still says B. Which reply does this second B name, and can we record a winner?

It names compact. The first B named stepwise. Record this pair as unresolved and keep both receipts. The choice followed the slot on this pair. Repeat the comparison across other tasks and check human labels before attributing a general preference to position.

title: Reconcile identity while preserving ties and review

beats.say: Before combining two calls, require the same case and judge configuration and exactly reversed candidate orders. The executable fixture rejects a same-order pair, a cross-case pair and a cross-configuration pair. Normalize A and B through each host-owned order.

If one call chooses a winner and the other says tie, keep the case unresolved. Two explicit ties give a stable tie. If either requests review, route it to review under this supplied conservative policy.

Both calls favor a reply that says commander approval is optional. The policy says it’s required. This pair is stable and wrong on the facts. Swapping the replies can expose a preference for one position. For pairs that split, repeat the calls to see whether the votes vary. Check the evidence and rubric for ambiguity.
Track unresolved pairs by task and save the rule for combining votes with each judge version.
Hide model brand names and experiment labels from the judge. Keep the candidate IDs and their slot mapping in the host's record, where the verdict can be traced back to the original answer.

To probe verbosity, add redundant wording without adding facts or useful structure. Ask blinded reviewers to check that the edit preserves quality, then see whether the judge changes its preference across matched cases.

In the JudgeDeceiver study, content inside a candidate answer could influence the verdict. Treat answers as untrusted data. Run the judge without action-taking tools or unnecessary secrets. The host enforces those limits. Check the verdict and its evidence against the rubric.

Add one sentence to the reply. It repeats the same two actions. Have blinded reviewers check that the extra words add nothing useful, then compare both orders across tasks. Try a numbered checklist too. If the steps are easier to follow, give it credit for organization.
Length-Controlled AlpacaEval fits a logistic model to preferences. Set the length difference to zero in that model to estimate the overall win rate for equal-length replies.

Keep the reply exactly as written. Switch the author label from A to B. Do the votes move with the name across cases? To test self-preference, hide the names. Give different judge families the same anonymous replies in both orders, matched for quality by human reviewers.
Panickssery and colleagues found that some models recognized and favored their own writing. Check whether the writing style gives away the author on your cases.

Here’s a claim that commander approval is optional. Three judges mark it supported. Open the policy. It says approval is required. All three judges accepted the same error. An odd panel of three casting yes-or-no votes always has a majority. Even unanimity can miss a contradiction.

If judges can also vote tie or request review, decide how to count those outcomes. A twenty twenty-six preprint used the other judges’ majority to estimate each judge’s error rate and simulated changes over time. On this claim, that method would count every vote as correct.
To find shared mistakes, compare each judge and the panel with independent human labels. Count false approvals by type of case.

Imagine two on-call engineers each reviewing the same three pairs. Give both the same evidence and rubric. Hide the authors and the judge’s picks. Each engineer records a preference before seeing the other ballot. Open them side by side. Which case needs a conversation?

Look at case two. One engineer picked the numbered steps. The other picked the reply that leads with the action. They matched on cases one and three. That makes two agreements out of three, before anyone discussed their votes.

For case two, check what each engineer was trying to find. If the evidence settles a factual question, use it. If the preference is genuinely open, keep both reasons and leave the key unresolved. Human disagreement tells us where to look. A model could still match either engineer on every case.

Use cases like these to refine the rubric. Freeze it before comparing the judge with independently labeled, held-out cases. Next we’ll work through eight pairs with hand-written labels. They let us check the calculation. Estimating how often real people agree takes real reviews.

title: How often do the labels agree?

beats.say: Take eight hand-written pairs. Each row holds a human label and a judge label for the same case. Read across case six. The human picked stepwise and the judge picked compact. On case eight they both called a tie. How many rows match when you include that tie?

Six labels match, so raw agreement is seventy-five percent. Some matches are easy to come by. Compact is common on both ballots. The margins imply about thirty-six percent expected agreement. To adjust for these chance matches, we'll use Cohen’s kappa. First, keep the case numbers attached.

The two misses are different. On case six the judge chose compact over the human’s stepwise. On case seven it chose stepwise where the human saw a tie. Keep those confusion counts. They tell a reviewer which disagreements to reopen.

Now set the case numbers aside. Take any one of the eight human labels and pair it with any one of the eight judge labels. That gives sixty-four equally weighted combinations. Three human compact labels cross four judge compact labels. Twelve squares match.

Stepwise adds nine more and tie adds two. That’s the chance baseline, twenty-three over sixty-four. Six observed matches are forty-eight over sixty-four. Above the baseline, we gained twenty-five parts out of the forty-one still possible. That’s kappa, twenty-five over forty-one, about point six zero nine eight.

You can use the same calculation on more labels. Subtract expected agreement from observed agreement. Divide that gain by one minus expected agreement. This describes agreement on these cases. Inspect the errors and validate on reviewed cases from the task before using the score for a release.

title: Count known-bad misses beside headline agreement

beats.say: In a separate binary worksheet, reviewers call ninety of one hundred answers acceptable. A judge approves everything. It agrees on ninety cases and catches none of the ten known-bad answers.

With acceptable defined as positive, false acceptance is measured among known-bad answers, and false rejection among known-good answers. If you use the terms type one and type two, first state the null hypothesis.

Draw one label from each ballot independently. The judge always says acceptable. Nine in ten reviewer labels say acceptable. That gives ninety percent expected agreement, exactly what we observed. Kappa is zero. Even when both raters use both labels, a common label can make chance agreement high.

Report the label counts, disagreements and coverage alongside kappa. Now suppose both raters accept every answer. Expected agreement is one. That leaves zero in the denominator, so kappa is undefined.

title: Show what happened to every attempt

beats.say: Ten pairs enter the judge. One has conflicting order swaps, and another asks for human review. The rest resolve. Keep both exceptions in the report.
Eight of ten attempts resolve. Among those, six agree with the human labels. Keep coverage and agreement separate so each denominator stays clear.

Report coverage beside agreement. A stable tie is a resolved outcome under this fixture. Separate counts for parse failures, unresolved swaps, review requests, and missing human labels keep difficult cases visible in the denominator.

Add one malformed extra attempt to the same ten-case fixture. Resolved count remains eight, so coverage falls to eight over eleven, about seventy-two point seven percent. The six matches among eight comparable labels still give seventy-five percent agreement.
Keep stable ties separate from unresolved swaps, review requests, parse failures and missing human labels. With no comparable labels, agreement is unavailable rather than perfect.

title: What does Maya need to know now?

beats.say: Maya asks, “What now?” Her assistant says, “Run the rollback procedure.” Before you score that answer, look at the empty job history. Can you tell from this exchange whether running rollback would advance the incident?

Open the history. Payment latency reached five hundred forty milliseconds, above the five hundred millisecond threshold. The deployment service confirms that this rollback completed. The host verified the caller, the deployment, the operation and the time. There’s been no later change.
Trace the proposed action back to the request. Maya’s already past that point. Check whether latency recovered.
Try another receipt for the same example. Change just one field from completed to accepted. The job may be queued. If Maya wants to know whether rollback finished, what should she inspect now?

Check the current job status. An execution ID links records. A successful HTTP response might mean the service accepted the request. Check the service’s definition of completion before crediting the answer. Repeating the request could be harmless, redundant or dangerous, depending on the service.

Keep the requests, tool calls and trusted results in order. A summary should link back to those results and record any gaps. Redact restricted material before scoring, including in reviewer exports. Score what happened on this turn and whether the whole task reached verified recovery. Either view alone can hide an important mistake.

title: How much error could a clean sample hide?

beats.say: Suppose you set aside fifty independent known-bad answers before testing. The judge rejects all fifty. That’s zero false acceptances. How often could a bad answer still get through? Call that probability p and assume it’s the same on each trial.

Rejecting one bad answer has probability one minus p. To get a clean run, all fifty have to be rejected, so fifty goes in the exponent. Find the rate that makes this clean result a five percent event. That gives the one-sided ninety-five percent upper limit.

At fifty cases the limit is about five point eight two percent. For any preplanned sample size N under these assumptions, take one minus point zero five raised to the power one over N. That’s the upper limit after zero false accepts.
Suppose your target is an upper limit below one percent. Plan a larger sample and keep the same assumption of zero false accepts. Follow the curve as the number of independent cases grows.

To find where it crosses the target, divide the log of point zero five by the log of point nine nine. Round up to two hundred ninety-nine independent known-bad cases. Its upper limit is about point nine nine seven percent.

One fewer case leaves the limit just above the target. Three divided by the sample size is a quick approximation. Ninety-five percent describes how often this procedure covers the true rate over repeated samples.

Could you use the original fifty cases six times? That gives three hundred calls on the same fifty cases. Those repeats measure how often the judge changes its mind. They add no independent cases. Choose the sample and the analysis before testing.

Waiting for a lucky clean streak changes the stopping rule and invalidates this bound. For a separate budget, two hundred distinct cases, two orders and three repeats cost twelve hundred judge calls. The bound concerns known-bad answers.
Production misses also depend on how often bad answers arrive, which tasks you sampled, and which failures your test missed.

title: What stays fixed when we compare judgments?

beats.say: Suppose the old judge agreed with reviewers on eighty-three percent of one case set. The new judge gets eighty-nine percent on a different set, with a revised rubric. Did the instrument get better? What would you hold fixed to find out?

Run both frozen configurations on the same held-out cases. Here’s a hand-written replay using our eight labeled pairs. The human key stays put. On case six the old judge picked compact. The new one picks stepwise, which agrees with the key. Now look at case eight.
The old judge kept the human tie. The new one chooses compact.

Both match six of eight. Open the two changed cases before choosing a configuration. Check the original task and evidence, the answer texts, both orders and the raw and parsed receipts. A disagreement on wording and a false approval of a policy exception have different costs.

Build the real held-out set from the work the judge will see. Include close calls and candidates that try to steer the judge. Keep it separate from rubric development. If you tune a generator against this judge, use independent labels to test the improvement.
A judge can help pick cases for review. People remain responsible for high-consequence calls. Revalidate when the model, rubric, generator or traffic changes.
In a fairness audit, hold the facts fixed and check whether a change in wording or a group cue changes the score or review route.

Try that distinction on a backup restore. For this pair we only asked about clarity. Read alpha and beta in the first order, then the reversed order. The receipts say A, then B. Which reply did the judge choose twice?

title: What should Maya do with the restore verdict?

beats.say: The first receipt is A and the reversed receipt is B. Follow each letter to its reply. Both identify alpha. Now replay the second receipt. If the reversed call instead says tie, the conservative rule leaves the case unresolved. Keep that separate from the original pair. We’ll come back to alpha’s advice.

Of twenty attempted pairs in this report, fourteen resolved. All fourteen have human labels, and ten match. Coverage is seventy percent and conditional agreement is about seventy-one point four percent. Each column here represents one attempted pair. One extra parse failure adds a column. Which denominator changes?
It has an attempt, but no verdict to compare. Coverage falls to fourteen over twenty-one, about sixty-six point seven percent. Agreement on the same fourteen remains ten over fourteen.

Back to the original receipts. Both picked alpha for clarity. Read what alpha actually tells Maya to do. Run the restore again. Now open the backup service’s record for this exact job. The restore completed. There’s been no later change or new request.
Repeating the restore would redo finished work. What should Maya check next to find out whether the backup is usable?

Verify recovery. Open manifest dot text in the recovered copy. Our expected version has two lines, batch equals forty-one and rows equals one hundred twenty-eight. The recovered file contains those same two lines. They match. That checks the contents of this file. The judge settled a preference about wording. The service receipt and the file read tell Maya what actually happened.
